title: Historic Deal Positions FIA World Endurance Championship for Record Decade of Growth as the Sport Enters its Golden Age
summary: Sport news The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), the founder and organiser of the 24 Hours of Le Mans, have today announced a major deal for the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), securing another decade of growth.   The landmark agreement, which comes during a period of unprecedented growth for the championship, will ensure a common ambition to expand the partnership and drive its commercial success. It will run from the end of 2027, when the current agreement expires, to the end of 2037.    Under the extended partnership agreement, all regulatory processes will be overseen by FIA Working Groups, the FIA Endurance Commission, and will require the final approval of the FIA World Motor Sport Council. The homologation process has also been streamlined, with the FIA and ACO overseeing the homologation of all cars competing in the Hypercar class.   The renewed partnership will also deliver significantly increased branding for the FIA. This includes enhanced branding prominently displayed across key areas including parc fermé, the podium and the Safety Cars, as well as across broadcast coverage.   With an expanding fanbase, a wider pool of competitors, and a global calendar of iconic events, the championship is stronger than ever. Since its inception in 2012, it has set the global standard for long-distance circuit racing. Following the introduction of the Hypercar regulations in 2021, interest in the championship from motor sport fans and from the automotive world has surged.    FIA WEC’s trackside audience has grown 8% so far in 2026, with millions of fans following the championship globally. The fanbase for the championship is also evolving. This year, 44% of attendees are aged 34 or younger, while 40% are attending an FIA WEC event for the first time. The championship has secured the long-term loyalty of its existing fanbase, while building the next generation of endurance racing fans.   Eight of the world’s leading auto-manufacturers currently compete in Hypercar, the top category of FIA WEC. Following the addition of the LMGT3 class in 2024, the championship now counts no fewer than 14 marques in total on the starting grid. Two more giants of the automotive industry – Ford and McLaren – are set to join the Hypercar ranks in 2027.   For over 100 years, endurance racing has served as a proven testbed for technologies that transfer from track to road. This renewed agreement creates a solid framework for advancing hydrogen powertrains in competition, providing a clear pathway toward more sustainable transport and mobility.    It will also deliver a more unified technical framework that defines top-level endurance racing Hypercars competing both in the FIA WEC and IMSA in North America, which will be introduced from 2030.  The new framework will provide greater cost-efficiency for manufacturers to compete in endurance racing championships and events globally, boosting potential participation and increasing the spectacle for motor sport fans.   With interest in FIA WEC at levels never seen before, the championship is positioned for continued growth and success over the coming decade. This new deal offers the solid foundation needed to secure its future, marking a milestone moment in the history of FIA WEC.    Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA , said:  “This is not simply an agreement, it is a vital step forward for racing that will secure the future of the FIA World Endurance Championship for years to come.     “This is a deal built for the future, a deal of the century, one that strengthens the collaboration between the FIA and ACO, a relationship that dates back over 120 years, and sets the championship up for a decade of record growth that will deliver real benefits to fans, drivers, teams and manufacturers.     “It has been an honour to play a part in the collaboration that has helped usher in this golden age of endurance racing. I look forward to continuing our work alongside President Pierre Fillon and his team as we build on this momentum and shape an even stronger future.”     Pierre Fillon, President of the Automobile Club de l'Ouest , said: “ We are delighted to see the agreement between the FIA and the ACO extended, reinforcing the strong and long-standing relationship that has been at the heart of the FIA World Endurance Championship since its creation in 2012. This partnership has been built on trust, shared ambition, and a common commitment to the development of endurance racing.      “Together, the FIA and the ACO have created a solid foundation for the continued success and international growth of the championship, and we look forward to writing the next chapter of this remarkable collaboration. Finally, I would like to thank FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem for the great relationship we have built.”      Alberto Villarreal, General Manager at the FIA , said:  “The FIA World Endurance Championship is stronger and more popular than it has ever been before, with a growing and evolving fanbase, and an impressive roster of top-tier global auto-manufacturers.      “The agreement announced today underlines the investment in the championship from both the FIA and the ACO, and our commitment to continue bringing the sport to new audiences. It is a pivotal moment in the history of FIA WEC, and provides the foundation and stability needed for the championship’s ongoing success.”      Frédéric Lequien, CEO of the Le Mans Endurance Management, the promoter for the FIA World Endurance Championship , said:  “This agreement comes at an exciting time for the FIA World Endurance Championship. The championship is experiencing exceptional momentum, with growing engagement from manufacturers, teams, partners, media, and fans around the world. The extension provides a strong framework to build on this growth, further strengthen the global appeal of the WEC and continue to deliver a world-class championship at the forefront of endurance racing. We are looking forward to an ambitious and exciting future for the FIA WEC.”     -   Notes to Editors     The renewed agreement between the FIA and the ACO follows three other significant long-term agreement announcements since July 2025:      FIA and Formula E sign landmark extension to power Formula E World Championship for another 10 years, announced in July 2025 –  information here        Multi-year Concorde Governance Agreement between the FIA, Formula 1 Group and all 11 race teams, announced in December 2025 –  information here        “Deal of the Century” for FIA World and European Rally Championships in July 2026 –  information here         These announcements form part of the FIA’s strategic investment in the future of motor sport, as it continues its mission to grow participation in the sport and provide a safe and accessible platform for all.      The FIA has seen a radical transformation since 2021, and earlier this year  announced  that it had delivered its strongest set of financial results in a decade in 2025, with an operating profit of €6.7m. It also reported an exceptional gain of €20m through the Formula E contract extension.    About the FIA  The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.   Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.    About the ACO   Founded in 1906, the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO) is the creator and organiser of major motorsport events: the first Grand Prix in history in 1906, followed by the 24 Hours of Le Mans starting in 1923. The ACO has also been the organiser and promoter of the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC) since 2012 and the creator of continental series: the European Le Mans Series (2004) and the Asian Le Mans Series (2013). The ACO organises the 24 Hours of Le Mans Motorcycle Race, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Karting, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Truck Race, and the French Motorcycle Grand Prix on its Le Mans circuits…   The 24 Hours of Le Mans serves as a true technological laboratory focused on automotive innovation. It is in this spirit that the ACO continues to evolve. Sustainable mobility - embodied in particular by MissionH24, which aims to introduce hydrogen to the 24 Hours of Le Mans - is a key objective for the ACO.   Since 2024, the ACO has held the FIA’s 3-star environmental accreditation and is ISO 20121 certified, the benchmark for responsible event management. In September 2024, the 24 Hours of Le Mans circuit was also voted “France’s Favourite Monument.”    About FIA WEC  The FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), created in 2012 by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), represents the undisputed pinnacle of the long-distance discipline.   Bringing together the world’s leading manufacturers, biggest brands, top drivers and most successful teams, FIA WEC races around the globe, pushing the limits of speed, performance and durability while encouraging ever-greater feats of strategic skill. If the fast and fearless drivers are the heroes, then the cars are the stars, from their cutting-edge technology to their dynamic design. And then, of course, there is the sound of the engines – that uncompromising, unadulterated roar.   The cornerstone of the calendar is the iconic 24 Hours of Le Mans, an event born in 1923 that continues to serve as the ultimate test for manufacturers seeking to prove their mettle – but every race has its own character, challenges and pitfalls. As a series with a proud history, a compelling present and a thrilling future, FIA WEC remains endurance racing’s global benchmark, continuously setting the standard in the sport and inspiring generations to come. title: FIA Asia Pacific Congress to Bring Member Clubs Together in the Philippines to Advance Mobility and Motor Sport Across the Region
summary: Members news    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, will be hosted by the Automobile Association Philippines (AAP) in Boracay in the Philippines for its Asia Pacific Congress next week, bringing together FIA Member Clubs from across the region.  From 29 September to 1 October, 120 delegates from Member Clubs across Asia and the Pacific, will unite in Boracay for three days of collaboration, innovation and knowledge sharing. Throughout the week, attendees will discuss priorities to advance safe and sustainable mobility for road users and drive greater motor sport accessibility.  The Asia-Pacific region is one of the FIA's most diverse and dynamic, spanning some of the world's fastest-growing mobility markets and an expanding motor sport community. The Congress will provide Member Clubs with an opportunity to share expertise and develop practical solutions which respond to the specific needs of their members and communities.  Across mobility, discussions will focus on road safety, innovation, sustainable and accessible transport, tourism and the changing needs of road users, building on the FIA's work to support Clubs in delivering meaningful impact at a national and regional level.  Motor sport sessions will explore opportunities to increase participation, strengthen grassroots competition and create more accessible pathways into the sport, supporting the FIA's ambition to make motor sport more affordable and accessible around the world.  The programme will also showcase the work and innovation of FIA Member Clubs across Asia-Pacific, providing a platform to share successful initiatives which can be adapted and scaled across the region.   H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said:   "The Asia-Pacific region is central to the future of both mobility and motor sport, and our Member Clubs are at the heart of that progress.   From improving road safety and embracing innovation to creating new opportunities for people to participate in motor sport, our Clubs are delivering real impact for their communities.    "The FIA Asia Pacific Congress gives us an important opportunity to bring that expertise together, share ideas and strengthen collaboration across one of the most diverse and dynamic regions in our Federation.    "I thank our hosts the Automobile Association Philippines, and President Joe Ferreria, for welcoming the FIA family to Boracay and look forward to another productive Congress."    FIA Region II President and President of host club the Automobile Association Philippines, Augustus ‘Joe’ Ferreria said:   "The strength of this region comes from the diversity, knowledge and ambition of our Member Clubs. Bringing our community together in the Philippines gives us the opportunity to learn from one another, identify shared challenges and develop solutions that can support Clubs across the region.    "The Asia Pacific Congress is an important moment for us to build on the progress already being made and ensure our Clubs have the tools, knowledge and connections they need to continue growing.    "We are proud to welcome the FIA and our fellow Member Clubs from across Asia-Pacific to the Philippines.”   The Congress follows a period of significant activity for the FIA across the region.  The FIA has expanded its  Safe Mobility 4 All & 4 Life  programme into Asia-Pacific, supporting Member Clubs and authorities with training and practical tools to improve road safety, while initiatives including the  FIA Innovation Challenge  continue to showcase Club-led solutions which can be shared and scaled across the Federation.  Across motor sport, the region continues to play an important role at every level of competition, from grassroots participation and regional championships through to the FIA's major World Championships with Malaysia set to host the Bahrain Grand Prix in the days following the congress.  The FIA Member Club structure forms the backbone of the federation’s governance and operations, with each full Member Club holding voting rights across the FIA’s elections and regulatory decisions. Clubs are grouped into two primary categories, with some serving in both roles:   Mobility Clubs – provide mobility services and represent the interest of road users, with a focus on road safety, travel and tourism, consumer rights, and sustainable mobility  National Sporting Authorities (ASNs) – govern and develop motorsport at a national level, are responsible for sporting events, issuing licenses, and engagement across regulations   Within the FIA there are four Mobility Regions and 6 sport zones. The FIA Asia Pacific Congress will welcome Member Clubs from across the region. The global FIA Membership is comprised of 246 clubs across five continents, connecting over 80 million members.      -ENDS-      For media enquiries please contact:   Geri Sherwin, Director of Presidential and Mobility Communications:  gsherwin@fia.com   George Mitchell, Mobility Communications Officer:  gmitchell@fia.com        About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem meets with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev as Baku Celebrates a Decade of Racing
summary: FIA news His Excellency Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), met with His Excellency Ilham Aliyev, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, in Baku today to discuss shared priorities across motorsport and mobility.  The meeting, which took place during the Baku Grand Prix as the city celebrated a decade of racing on its iconic streets, provided an opportunity to discuss Azerbaijan’s continued development as a major international sporting destination, its established position within global motorsport, and opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the country and the FIA.  Azerbaijan has become an important destination on the international sporting calendar, with Baku providing one of Formula 1’s most distinctive city-centre settings and attracting fans and visitors from around the world.  The Presidents also discussed the wider role of mobility in supporting economic growth and connectivity, as well as the importance of road safety and sustainable transport as Azerbaijan continues to invest in its infrastructure and international connectivity.   FIA President, H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:   “It was a pleasure to meet with His Excellency President Ilham Aliyev and discuss our shared ambitions for the continued development of motorsport and mobility in Azerbaijan.    “The success of Formula 1 in Baku demonstrates what can be achieved through long-term commitment, strong organisation and a clear vision for the role that major sporting events can play in bringing people together and showcasing a country to the world. My congratulations on a fantastic ten years of racing and I look forward to many more.    “Our discussions also extended beyond motorsport. As the global federation for mobility organisations, the FIA is committed to working with governments and our Member Clubs such as the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation to make mobility safer, more accessible and more sustainable. I look forward to continuing our collaboration with our partners in Azerbaijan across these important areas.”   President Ben Sulayem’s visit comes as the FIA continues to strengthen its engagement across the region through its global network of Member Clubs and partners, including the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation and its President Anar Alakbarov.  The FIA has placed significant emphasis on growing motorsport participation and strengthening the pathway from grassroots competition to the highest levels of the sport, while using its global mobility network to advance road safety, sustainable mobility and accessibility. Azerbaijan’s position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, alongside continued investment in transport and infrastructure, provides opportunities for further collaboration across both pillars of the FIA’s work.  The meeting formed part of President Ben Sulayem’s programme in Azerbaijan, bringing together government, motorsport and mobility stakeholders to discuss opportunities to further develop the FIA’s activities in the country and wider region.        ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. title: WEC: Alpine on pole at Fuji after rain leads to qualifying cancellation
summary: Sport news Heavy rain swept across Fuji Speedway ahead of the scheduled start of the LMGT3 qualifying session, which began on time but was red-flagged after François Heriau went off in his #21 VISTA AF Corse Ferrari.  The decision was then taken to cancel the remaining qualifying sessions due to the forecast of heavier rain and fog at Fuji Speedway.  That meant that, in accordance with the regulations, the grid was set according to the best times from the three Free Practice sessions held across Friday and Saturday morning.  Victor Martins’ FP2 time of 1m40.594s ensured that the #36 Alpine will start from pole position, marking the first-ever WEC pole for the A424 Hypercar.  It was a double celebration for the French manufacturer as the #35 car will join its sister Hypercar on the front row, putting Alpine in a strong position to defend last year’s victory at the venue.  Second on the grid should initially have been the #007 Aston Martin Valkyrie, but it was demoted to fourth after receiving a penalty for causing a collision in the morning’s FP3 session.  Starting third on the grid will be the #17 Genesis Magma Hypercar, meaning the Korean manufacturer will begin tomorrow’s race from by far its best-ever starting position.  In the LMGT3 category, the #77 Proton Competition Ford Mustang will start from pole position after setting the fastest FP2 time on Friday afternoon. It marks the first pole position for a Ford Mustang since the Lone Star Le Mans race at COTA in September 2025.       WEC  Endurance  6 Hours of Fuji  WEC   Sport 1SportWECWECEndurance6 Hours of Fuji00 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am

title: Goodyear FIA ETRC Jarama day one round-up: Smith joins Kiss in the Winners’ Club with maiden victory
summary: Sport news After finishing second overall at Le Mans last Sunday, Smith led Race 2 at Circuito de Madrid Jarama – RACE this evening from the front to triumph ahead of José Eduardo Rodrigues and local hero Antonio Albacete, who took third.  Smith also banked top Chrome category honours in Race 2 with Lukas Hahn taking second followed by title rivals Mark Taylor and John Newell.  Earlier, eight-time champion* Norbert Kiss scored his 19th win of another hugely impressive season from his 13th pole position of 2026. Jochen Hahn took second with Sascha Lenz finishing third. Lukas Hahn captured Chrome glory in Race 1 ahead of Smith and Newell.    Flash reports from Race 1 and Race 2 are available at the links below. Revisit Race 1 and Race 2 on   YouTube  .   Race 1 :  https://www.goodyearfiaetrc.com/news/start-to-finish-kiss-and-lukas-hahn-on-a-high-in-goodyear-fia-etrc    Race 2:    https://www.goodyearfiaetrc.com/news/smith-joins-the-list-of-goodyear-fia-etrc-winners-with-maiden-victory     Race 1 winner Norbert Kiss said:  “It was a good victory, we had good pace. The start was a bit strange because the green came really late and I barely see the lights anymore because I was so close to the lights, almost underneath. But, okay, we came through, good first turn and start to build the gap a bit. A good race, we were fast, so again, a good job from the team, Révész Racing. The truck was working very nice, everything was nice. We were confident, we had the pace and I pushed a little bit in the first two laps. I see Jochen cannot keep up so it was nice.”   Race 1 Chrome winner Lukas Hahn said:  ““It was a really good race. We had a good start and Antonio was in front of me and José behind me. It was good, we had nearly all the same pace so it was hard, so for me it was just to save the position because I was first in Chrome. All was fine, I enjoyed and the truck was really good. It’s really difficult to overtake fair but I needed to watch for the Chrome championship and we are really happy, all was perfect.”     Race 2 overall and Chrome winner Bradley Smith said:  “ “It’s really good, we had a good start and I managed to hold the lead. Once we got out of there José wouldn’t let me breathe through the whole race. Lap after lap, it was the longest race of my life, but eventually we got it done and I’m really happy. Towards the later part my truck went off a bit because I was pushing so hard at the start and they were putting pressure on me. title: F1 – Verstappen storms to first pole of 2026 at Sepang as Hamilton hands Ferrari front row start
summary: Sport news Max Verstappen claimed his first pole position of the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship with a commanding performance in Qualifying for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, beating Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar at the Sepang International Circuit.  The Dutchman delivered a final lap of 1:35.130 to secure the 49th pole position of his career, finishing 0.298s clear of Hamilton, with Hadjar third in thre session. However, the French driver will take a five-place penalty for the race due an Internal Combustion Engine change and will drop to P8 on the grid.   Verstappen had already established himself as the driver to beat by topping all three practice sessions and continued that form throughout Qualifying to secure his first pole since the 2025 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.  At the top of the hour, Haas drivers Esteban Ocon and Ollie Bearman were first on track. Elsewhere, Ferrari and Audi opted for Medium compound tyres as they looked to save sets of Softs.   Championship leader Kimi Antonelli set the early benchmark of 1:37.041 on the red-banded Softs, before Verstappen moved clear by half a second. Hadjar followed his team-mate into second, although Hamilton and Charles Leclerc subsequently demonstrated the competitiveness of the medium compound by moving into the top three.  At the other end of the order, Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg dropped out of the session in P17 ahead of Bearman while the Briton’s outgoing team-mate Esteban Ocon qualified 19th ahead of Williams’ Alex Albon and the Cadillacs of Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Pérez.  In the second session Verstappen lowered the benchmark to 1:35.696, becoming the first driver to break through the 1m36s barrier. Leclerc followed, two tenths adrift, while Antonelli had a lap deleted for exceeding track limits at Turn 6.  The Mercedes driver was forced to return to the circuit on a fresh set of soft tyres, leaving him with fewer new compounds available for Q3. His subsequent effort was sufficient to secure progression, but the additional running would prove significant later in the session.  At the other end of the order, Racing Bulls faced a battle to keep both cars in contention. Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad, already facing a back-row start following a power unit change, provided a tow for Liam Lawson rather than setting a representative lap himself.  Lawson moved into the top 10, only for Gabriel Bortoleto to produce a late improvement to dump the New Zealander out of Q3 by 0.209s. Lawson was eliminated alongside Fernando Alonso, Carlos Sainz, Lance Stroll, Franco Colapinto and Lindblad.  Colapinto is also facing a grid penalty, of 15 places, due to causing a collision in Baku and 10 for a power unit change. Lindblad will also start from the back following his own penalty.  In Q3, Mercedes’ George Russell was first to establish a competitive time, but his 1:36.032 was quickly eclipsed by Hadjar, before Hamilton and Leclerc moved into second and third respectively.  Verstappen then delivered a 1:35.250 to take provisional pole, opening a 0.308s advantage over his team-mate. Oscar Piastri split the Ferrari drivers, while Lando Norris moved into sixth. Antonelli delayed his sole attempt until the other drivers had completed their opening runs, but the championship leader could not match Verstappen's pace. His 1:35.631 placed him third provisionally.   Verstappen returned to the circuit for one final attempt, initially unable to improve in the first two sectors. However, a strong final sector brought a further 0.120s improvement, taking him to 1:35.130 and confirming pole position.  Hamilton also found time on his final lap, securing second place with a 1:35.428 and giving Ferrari a place on the front row. Hadjar was unable to improve and finished third on the timesheets with a 1:35.558, but his five-place penalty will drop him to eighth on the starting grid.  Antonelli therefore inherits third place, ahead of Leclerc, who recorded a 1:35.666. Norris finished sixth with a 1:35.757, narrowly ahead of McLaren team-mate Piastri, whose 1:35.762 left the pair separated by just 0.005s.  Russell completed the top eight, 0.741s off pole, while Pierre Gasly secured ninth for Alpine and Bortoleto completed the top 10 for Audi.   2026 FIA Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – Qualifying  1 Max Verstappen Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 1:35.130 - - 2 Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 1:35.428 0.298 0.313 3 Isack Hadjar Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 1:35.558 0.428  4 Kimi Antonelli Mercedes 1:35.631 0.501  5 Charles Leclerc Ferrari 1:35.666 0.536  6 Lando Norris McLaren/Mercedes 1:35.757 0.627  7 Oscar Piastri McLaren/Mercedes 1:35.762 0.632  8 George Russell Mercedes 1:35.871 0.741  9 Pierre Gasly Alpine/Mercedes 1:37.210 2.080  10 Gabriel Bortoleto Audi 1:37.673 2.543  11 Liam Lawson Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1:37.023 1.893  12 Fernando Alonso Aston Martin/Honda 1:37.220 2.090  13 Carlos Sainz Williams/Mercedes 1:37.527 2.397  14 Lance Stroll Aston Martin/Honda 1:37.566 2.436  15 Franco Colapinto Alpine/Mercedes - - - 16 Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford - - - 17 Nico Hülkenberg Audi 1:37.970 2.840  18 Oliver Bearman Haas/Ferrari 1:37.980 2.850  19 Esteban Ocon Haas/Ferrari 1:38.233 3.103  20 Alexander Albon Williams/Mercedes 1:38.600 3.470  21 Valtteri Bottas Cadillac/Ferrari 1:38.611 3.481 22 Sergio Pérez Cadillac/Ferrari 1:38.933 3.803           FIA Formula One World Championship    F1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026F101 Saturday, October 3, 2026 - 1:09pm  Saturday, October 3, 2026 - 1:09pm

title: F1 - 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia Post-Qualifying Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS   1 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)    2 – Lewis HAMILTON (Ferrari)    3 – Isack HADJAR (Red Bull Racing)     PARC FERMÉ INTERVIEWS   (Conducted by Naomi Schiff)     Q: Max, huge congratulations. You’ve been looking quick all weekend so far, but to take pole position here for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, how good does that feel?   Max VERSTAPPEN:  It’s fantastic. I mean, we’ve been trying many Grands Prix, you know, to get pole, sometimes a bit closer than others, but to finally get it from where we started the season, pretty incredible.    Q: We know that there’s been a lot of talk about degradation around this track, but you guys have looked consistent both in single-lap pace as well as long-run data. I know you’re still hunting for your first Grand Prix victory of the season. Do you think this will be the place you’ll get it done?   MV:  I mean, I’m happy with today and for sure I’m going to try to win tomorrow. I mean, when you start first, that’s the target.    Q: Fantastic. Well, we’ll look forward to seeing that tomorrow. Max. Lewis, congratulations. A P2 after what didn’t look like a very straightforward weekend, but you’re one of the few, well, one of the ten drivers to come back to the circuit. How good is it to be back here?   Lewis HAMILTON:  Well, I mean, listen to this crowd, guys. This is, I think, the biggest crowd we’ve ever seen here, at least in my time of driving. But yeah, I love this energy. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It’s so hot here, I keep saying it, but that’s made it a massive challenge for the tyres, for the car, for the mechanics in the garage. And I’m really, really thankful to my team. We’ve made so many changes through all these practice sessions and because the cars are sliding, these tyres are overheating, it was really, really hard to find a good balance. And we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. So, to be able to close the gap to, you know, two or three tenths to Max, who’s been so quick all weekend, is great. And yeah, I’m so, so grateful.    Q: So, as you say, the heat is brutal out here at the moment. I can’t imagine what it’s like for the fans, but for you drivers as well in the cockpit, there’s a lot to juggle, with tyre temperatures and degradation on an abrasive surface like here. How much is that going to be a focus tomorrow, and are you happy with where your car is at going into tomorrow’s race?   LH:  Much happier with where the car is but tomorrow is a completely different ball game. Making these tyres last around this track, I mean, they’re overheating from the get-go. So, every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have, depending on the wind, makes a difference of how far you’re going to go. But I like to think we’ve got a good balance. These guys, you know, Max was really quick on his long runs, so we’ll just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow.    Q: Fantastic. We’ll look forward to seeing that tomorrow. Isack, congratulations. I think a lot of people were concerned about you spending some time out of the car. It looks like you may have had an upgrade to your wrist because you’ve been quick ever since your comeback. How good was it today?   Isack HADJAR:  Yeah, I mean, the car has been very good since last week, so, you know, it’s good to come back at such a time. And yeah, I’m enjoying it. You know, like fighting for a top three, even though it wasn’t my finest qualifying session, it’s a good feeling.    Q: Well, you say it wasn’t your finest qualifying session. It was enough for P3, but tomorrow, unfortunately, you have some penalties for a good start. So, are you going to be fighting through the field? Are you confident that you have a car that’s going to have some raceability tomorrow?   IH:  Yeah, it’s very unfortunate that we take the penalty on the track where we’re that fast, but, you know, from eighth I’m confident we can go through the field and come back for a good result.    PRESS CONFERENCE      Q: Max Verstappen, pole today. Fantastic result, your first pole of 2026 and the first pole without a Mercedes engine. Does that feel like a huge result for the team?   MV:  I think, in general, it’s been an incredible result for us. Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us. I think from FP1 we started quite well and from then onwards we’ve just been trying to improve the car further. It’s incredible, honestly. I’m very happy to be on pole here.    Q: So, last time you were here, you won. What’s going to stop you from winning tomorrow? Is it the heat, the tyre deg, the Ferraris? Are you expecting a challenge from anywhere else? The rain, maybe?   MV:  It’s tough always around here. It’s very hot, for ourselves, but also for the cars, for the brakes, for the tyres. So, yeah, the race is definitely going to be a tough one. You have to manage a lot and it’s impossible to know at the moment, of course, who can do that the best. But at the same time, also, there is a start, where a lot of things can happen. So, we just need to be aware, ready, and then we’ll see how competitive we are in the race. But so far this weekend, yes, I’ve felt good, I felt confident, and I hope we can show that again tomorrow.    Q: Lewis, if I can come to you. A fantastic lap. Is it a surprise to be on the front row?   LH:  Yes, definitely. Firstly, congrats to Max. He’s been so quick all weekend. We were kind of looking at fifth or sixth, throughout the weekend, in the ultimate pace compared to the rest. And we saw Mercedes come with a big upgrade and, considering they’ve been winning every race, thought the upgrade would really propel them even further forwards. But it’s just interesting to find ourselves here. The car felt great. We’ve made lots of changes. I think they’ve got a great package. Red Bull have obviously been making some great progress. I mean, the only place we lose is down the straights to them. I think we’re losing three or four tenths on the straights to them, which we know of, and so we just work as hard as we can to try and maximise in the corners. But I think we were able to do that today. So, this is really down to the mechanics and the engineers. We all did a really great job together, and then also execution was really on point. So, if we could keep this up, hopefully we can get better results moving forwards.    Q: Last time you were on the front row, in Barcelona, you won. Is that possible tomorrow? And how much of a boost is it that the changes you made worked and that the work that you’ve been doing has resulted in a great result today?   LH:  Yeah, I mean, the thing is that these cars are so sensitive. You make the smallest change and it’s ridiculous the difference it can make from one run, one session, to the other. One click of front wing, or one millimetre ride height, a quarter of a degree of camber, or 0.1 of toe, or something like that. These little things make such a big difference to balance, and it’s literally a moving target that you’re trying to work around with set-up and then also controls that we have. Even then, understanding throttle application. If you get to full throttle too early, you [inaudible] and you lose time down the straight. These kind of things that I don’t think many of us like, but mastering all that together is a massive challenge and obviously makes it even harder for us because I think we’re so on the edge, because we are losing so much on the straights. So, I’m just hoping that we continue to work hard. If we get to a point where we have base power with these guys, I think we’re going to have an even better fight in future.    Q: Great, thank you, Lewis. Isack, if I can come to you. You sounded frustrated on the radio with P3. Did you feel there was more out there for you today?   IH:  Second, I would say. You know, anything I can take to limit tomorrow’s penalty. Yeah, I just feel like it’s the first weekend that, after three free practice sessions, I feel like I need a bit more mileage because the laps are so limited here with the big tyre degradation. So basically, each compound, you get one lap of learning, each set of tyres, basically. I just feel like I worked quite well the whole weekend, but I feel like I wish there was another qualifying so I can keep improving the balance of the car, because I was not really satisfied with how we ended the session. And, yeah, had a few issues on that deployment on that last lap. So, all in all, nothing really aligned, and to come out in third with all these issues, on a normal weekend I would be P8 and now I’m third. So, we should be happy about the performance, but I’m not really.    Q: You mentioned on the radio a lot of understeer. That’s in order to protect the rears in the race tomorrow. So what have you learned from the long runs that gives you some confidence you’ll be able to get up and join these two pretty quickly from P8?   IH:  No, I mean, I don’t think I’m going to see them tomorrow because it’s quite dictated by your starting position. You may be super quick, then when you sit behind a car that’s still competitive... Tomorrow I’ll be fighting Mercedes, McLaren, Ferrari, so they are fast cars and it’s not like I’m going to run through them at all. So, in the end, I’m going to have to look after the tyres, make the most of the free air I get and try and climb.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Christian Menath – Motorsport-magazin.com) For Max and for Lewis. I guess you all made sacrifices for the long-run pace, but do you fear that the others made even bigger sacrifices and that you pay the price tomorrow in the race for your starting position? Max, do you want to take it?   MV:  Personally, I’m confident with what I did. If others make bigger sacrifices, then good luck to them, but I’m ready.  LH:  I mean, we just have to focus on ourselves. I don’t know what the others are doing. I think Max had really good long runs. Ours were okay, but I think the balance was a bit off. I think our car is better, hopefully, now for the race. So, yeah, I think we’re all in a similar ballpark because overtaking is not that easy here either. Even though we have these long straights, we’re all on SM, and following is quite difficult because we’re always overheating. It’ll be interesting tomorrow.    Q: (Jake Boxall-Legge – Autosport) A question for Max and for Isack, please. Max, you’ve kind of spoken about the progression of Red Bull through the season, but obviously one-three here is an amazing result for the team. What is it about the circuit that’s kind of brought this car to life, let’s say?   MV:  I don’t know. I mean, it’s always very hard to say why that is, but I think for us anyway, the last few races we have probably understood the car a little bit better, but also the upgrades have pushed some of the weaknesses out of the car. I mean, there are, of course, always things that you would still like, but we have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It’s simple as that. When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car. So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time. And then on a track probably where it’s all very hot and you want a, let’s say, stable balance or connected balance, then that’s very important. And that’s, I think, what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends.  IH:  Yeah, I mean, on my side, I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest. Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference. And, yeah, the last two weekends have been surprising. Even though I was following from close, even though I was on the bench, I feel like I’m quite surprised driving this car right now. I still believe there are things that need major improvements and still the car is performing okay, so it’s only good news. But, to be fair, I’m actually surprised it’s performing that well on a tarmac that has such low grip. Usually it doesn’t really suit our car, but apparently it does. So it’s good that it works in Baku and Sepang, two completely different tracks. I think it’s good news.    Q: (Riley Sullivan – FHM Australia) A question for Max. Where does this pole position rank for you all-time?   MV:  Honestly, I don’t remember them all. I mean, can you imagine? I’m not remembering them. Can you, Lewis? Do you remember them all? No, for sure not. There’s a few, you know. [To Isack] You don’t remember your poles? They’re coming, they’re coming. No, it was good, but it also sometimes depends a bit on the track. Sometimes it’s just easier to do a clean lap when the track is probably a bit cooler. Around here, when it’s hot, it’s also very easy to overstep it or have a little moment, and then you’re not very satisfied with it. So I find it sometimes just very hard to rank it because of track conditions as well. But at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter. It’s only your first, that’s what I care about. And sometimes, yes, it’s a bit easier, a bit better than others, but it was good enough.    Q: Is it the biggest surprise pole you’ve had, considering the upgrade Mercedes?   MV:  No, for sure not. I’ve had some shocking poles. But I think from everyone, I could say, “Okay, we might be in the running for it,” but then you never know how the other teams are operating. So you have to just wait and see until you get into qualifying. I mean, I was probably first in Q1, two and three, so then I think, yeah, there is a big opportunity to get it.    Q:   (Dzhastina Golopolosova – F1Maximaal.nl)   A question to Max. Max, some days ago you confirmed that you are going to race in Portimão, and Portimão will be the first time you and Valentino Rossi will race on the same grid. So does having him on the same grid add something extra to that weekend, or is the main attraction simply the opportunity to race?   MV:  Yeah, I hope I get to see him. He’s a very cool guy, so I hope to catch up with him. I mean, it’s nice, but I do not hope to see him in the race, so that’s normally a good sign. I actually hope to see no one, to be just up front and do a good job. But you never know. The grid is super competitive, so I’m just looking forward to the challenge. It’s very different to Formula 1, but I love it. I mean, I had my first taste already this year at the Nordschleife, and Portimão is a very cool track to drive. So I’m just going to enjoy it and, of course, as a team, we’ll try to do the best we can to get a good result out of it.    ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Saturday, October 3, 2026 - 11:57am  Saturday, October 3, 2026 - 11:57am

title: F1 – Antonelli tops final practice for Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
summary: Sport news Kimi Antonelli set the pace in Free Practice 3 for the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, leading Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar as Mercedes demonstrated its one-lap pace ahead of Qualifying at the Sepang International Circuit.  The Mercedes driver posted a fastest time of 1:36.302 to finish 0.278s clear of Verstappen, with Red Bull team-mate Hadjar third. George Russell completed the top four, 0.610s off the leading pace.  With track conditions remaining challenging, the opening phase of the session began quietly, with teams holding station out of the punishing midday heat. Charles Leclerc was among the first to venture out, on the Hard compound, and he set an initial benchmark of 1:37.772. Lando Norris then moved to the top of the timesheets on the Medium tyres with a 1:37.161.  Oscar Piastri followed his McLaren team-mate into second, while Mercedes and Red Bull initially remained in their garages.  The session was briefly interrupted when debris from Oliver Bearman's Haas was spotted at Turn 10, prompting Race Control to deploy the red flags. Following a four-minute stoppage to clear the circuit, the session resumed with a queue forming at the pit exit.  Antonelli immediately established himself at the front, setting a 1:36.924 on Soft tyres. Russell was 0.129s behind, while Verstappen moved into fourth on the medium compound, having encountered traffic in the final sector.  As the session progressed, Hadjar improved to 1:36.860 to briefly take the lead, but Antonelli and Verstappen responded to push the Red Bull driver down the order. Russell subsequently improved to 1:36.912, although he remained six tenths adrift of his team-mate.  McLaren's attempts to improve on the soft tyres proved less productive. Norris remained seventh after failing to complete a representative final sector, while Piastri also abandoned his final flying lap following a mistake.  Ferrari, meanwhile, completed its preparations with Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both finding improvements. Leclerc's 1:37.016 placed him fifth, just ahead of Hamilton, who finished 0.739s off Antonelli’s session topper. The Monegasque driver was the only competitor to use the Hard compound during the session, leaving him with one remaining set for the Grand Prix.  In the closing stages, Antonelli delivered the fastest lap of the weekend so far, stopping the clocks at 1:36.302 to secure top spot. Verstappen improved to second, 0.278s behind, while Hadjar retained third ahead of Russell.  The result marked Antonelli's first practice session at the head of the field since Madrid, with Mercedes appearing to have made further progress with its latest development package.  Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10, although both face grid penalties for Sunday's race.  Behind them, Gabriel Bortoleto was 11th for Audi, ahead of Fernando Alonso and Pierre Gasly. Esteban Ocon, Liam Lawson and Nico Hülkenberg followed, while Bearman, Carlos Sainz, Lance Stroll and Alexander Albon occupied positions 17 to 20. title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem Meets Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to Discuss Shared Motorsport Priorities
summary: FIA news Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, met with Lebanese President His Excellency Joseph Aoun today after attending the Rally of Lebanon, an event he won four times in a distinguished rally driving career which established him as a sporting ambassador for the Arab world.  The meeting at Baabda Palace provided an opportunity to reflect on the continued success of the event, and Lebanon’s position as a rallying stronghold in the Middle East.  Ben Sulayem accepted an official invitation from the Automobile and Touring Club of Lebanon and President Nabil ‘Billy’ Karam to attend the 48th Rally of Lebanon. The fourth round of this year’s FIA Middle East Rally Championship reached its finish at the ATCL in Kaslik, Jounieh last night (Sunday) with victory going to Lebanon’s Roger Feghali and co-driver Joseph Matar.   “I was pleased to meet with President Aoun and discuss our shared priorities for the future of motorsport,”   said FIA President Ben Sulayem.   “The Rally of Lebanon provided me with many great memories during my rally driving career, and I’m thrilled to once again experience the excitement this event creates for competitors and the country’s passionate motor sport fans.”    “The event has a rich history embedded in the origins of Middle East motorsport. It is firmly established as the home for asphalt rallying in the region, and plays a key role in our plans to ensure the long-term future of the FIA Middle East Rally Championship.    “Lebanon has always felt like a special place for me, and I want to thank the ATCL and its President, Nabil Karam, for their warm welcome and hospitality. I’m delighted to have met up again with some of the friends I have made at the club, and across the country over the years.”   Ben Sulayem’s legendary rally-driving achievements brought him widespread recognition, and he was awarded the President’s Cup by Lebanese President Amine Gemayel in 1987, and the Medal of Honour from Lebanese President Emile Lahoud in 1999.  Each of his four victories in the Rally of Lebanon, in 1987, 1991, 1998 and 1999, helped him secure the FIA Middle East Rally Championship title, which he won 14 times overall. He achieved the last three of those victories alongside his long-time co-driver Ronan Morgan.  Beyond his success in Middle East rallying, Ben Sulayem recorded his first overseas win in Turkey in 1991, and secured World Rally Championship Group N victories in Spain and Argentina over the following two years. He retired from competitive rallying in 2002.  In July, the FIA announced a landmark long-term commercial rights agreement for the FIA WRC and FIA European Rally Championship, following the acquisition of WRC Promoter GmbH by Cosmobilis and Park Square Capital. Designed to bring significant new investment into the sport, the biggest deal in the history of these championships supported the FIA’s vision under President Ben Sulayem, who said at the time:  “Rallying is a huge part of my personal story. It has shaped who I am and how I work, and I am deeply committed to its future.”       ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. title: New Book Maps Seven Forms of Online Abuse Threatening Sport
summary: FIA news The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, and Dublin City University (DCU) announce the publication of "Combating Online Abuse in Sports: The Game Beyond the Screen".    Supported by the FIA Foundation and FIA as part of its United Against Online Abuse initiative, and published by Palgrave Macmillan, the new open-access book challenges the idea that online abuse in sport begins and ends with hateful comments.    Bringing together experts from sport, sociology, media, law, cybersecurity, governance and digital business, it explores seven distinct forms of online abuse and examines how they affect a range of stakeholders including athletes, officials, journalists, organisations and the wider sporting community. The book was edited by Professor Theo Lynn (Dublin City University), Dr. Gary Sinclair (Dublin City University), Dr. Katie Liston (Ulster University) and Professor David Hassan (Ulster University).   The seven forms, most of which go unreported and unrecognised, are:     Toxic content: sustained abuse, threats and targeted pile-ons.       Content leakage: private images, medical records and personal data released without consent.       Overloading: coordinated campaigns that overwhelm accounts, inboxes, phone or other digital channels.       False reporting: malicious complaints or mass-reporting designed to damage reputations, disrupt performance and/or careers, or silence targets.       Digital impersonation: fake profiles, account hijacking, deepfakes and other attempts to assume or manipulate someone’s identity.       Surveillance: intrusive monitoring of movements, training patterns, communications, data or private life.       Lockout and control: attacks or restrictions that remove a target’s access to, or control over, their digital identity and communications.     A central message runs throughout the book: responsibility for tackling online abuse cannot simply be placed on athletes and other targets to become more "resilient". Meaningful progress requires coordinated action, stronger safeguarding, better digital security, greater platform governance and accountability, and coordinated action across sport, government, technology, and civil society.   The book is fully open access, ensuring it can be read, shared and used freely by athletes, sporting organisations, governing bodies, policymakers, platforms and researchers worldwide.    H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said:   "The FIA is committed to creating a safer digital environment for everyone in sport. This book, supported through our United Against Online Abuse campaign, provides the evidence base and practical framework that athletes, governing bodies and policymakers need to tackle online abuse in all its forms."     Professor Theo Lynn, Lead Editor and Executive Dean at DCU Business School, said:   “For too long, online abuse in sport has been treated as a problem of hateful comments. It is much bigger than that. Athletes can face deepfakes, leaked personal data, coordinated attacks, surveillance and even the loss of control of their own digital identity. If we cannot recognise these harms, we cannot tackle them. This book gives sport a common language for understanding the threat and a practical basis for action. By making it open access, we want that knowledge in the hands of everyone who can help make sport safer.”​     ENDS    For media enquiries please contact Maria Zander, Corporate Communications Manager:  mzander@fia.com      About United Against Online Abuse (UAOA)    Founded in 2023 by H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, the United Against Online Abuse (UAOA) coalition is an award-winning global initiative dedicated to combatting online abuse in sport through research, policy advocacy, and collaborative action. UAOA is endorsed by more than 75 governments, sports, academic institutions and technology organisations, and is supported by the FIA Foundation and co-funded by the European Union.      About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA)    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.    Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.     United Against Online Abuse   FIA 1FIAUnited Against Online Abuse00 Friday, October 2, 2026 - 5:10pm  Friday, October 2, 2026 - 5:10pm

title: ETRC: Chrome title chase takes centre stage at Jarama season finale
summary: Sport news Defending champion  Mark Taylor  trails  John Newell  by 13 points following an all-action visit to Le Mans last weekend with results in France determining that only British drivers Newell or Taylor can be Chrome champion for 2026.   “The title’s at stake but we just take each weekend as it comes,”  said Newell.  “I might be leading but it’s not job done [in the championship]. It starts again at Jarama, we just reset and go and make sure we have a good Saturday, then we should be on our way. I need to be fast. It’s a technical circuit, a very enjoyable circuit as well with lots of ups and downs where you can pick your places to overtake.”   Taylor, who became Chrome champion for the first time at Jarama last October, said:  “It’s going to be a tight and fun battle to the end. We’re cat and mousing on the points. We’ve just got to keep it on track, keep our fingers crossed and we’ll have no problems, It would be good to win but I don’t think about it. It’s whatever it’s going to be. If you think about it, you’re going to put pressure on yourself and then the mistakes come. In my mind it would be nice to win again, if we don’t, we don’t, no hardship, it’s motorsport and we’ll be back next season and push again.”   Despite winning his eighth overall Goodyear FIA ETRC title* at Le Mans,  Norbert Kiss  has no plans to slow down behind the wheel of his Révész Racing MAN when the season concludes in Spain.   “All the pressure is off, but we don’t lay back, we keep pushing because you’re only worth as much as your last race,”  said Hungarian Kiss.  “Jarama is a circuit I love, it’s been very good for us in the past with some very nice and very important victories. We try to do the maximum as well and enjoy maximum the weekend and enjoy the success of the season.”     Although top end-of-season Goodyear FIA ETRC silverware is out of reach for  Antonio Albacete  and  Luis Recuenco , the Spanish drivers have the honour of racing at home this weekend.  The 39th Grand Prix de España FIA Europeo de Camiones event is also the closest it gets to a home round for Portugal’s  José Eduardo Rodrigues , who made sure of the Goodyear FIA ETRC Young Driver crown* at Le Mans.  Six-time champion  Jochen Hahn  will battle Albacete and  Sascha Lenz  for the runner-up spot in the final Goodyear FIA ETRC title reckoning. Lenz is four points ahead of Hahn with Albacete 13 points adrift.   Lukas Hahn , who has been competing on a race-by-race basis this season, returns for the Jarama showdown. Jochen’s son was a race winner at Autodrom Most in August where he was also the recipient of the Goodyear Wingfoot Award, which is awarded at each round of the Goodyear FIA ETRC.   Steffi Halm  and  René Reinert , plus  Steffen Faas  and  Clemens Hecker  will compete at Le Mans this weekend as will  Luke Garrett  and  Bradley Smith , a double Chrome winner at Le Mans.  Multiple Finnish champion and FIA ETRC race winner  Mika Mäkinen  takes over the IVECO raced by his daughter, Emma, at Nürburgring and Autodrom Most earlier this season.  After banking two Goodyear FIA ETRC Chrome podiums at Circuit Zolder in mid-September,  Jonathan André  will be one to watch in his TotalEnergies-supported MAN.   THE GOODYEAR FIA ETRC IN SHORT  Combining the excitement of truck racing with entertainment, sustainability and technical innovation, the Goodyear FIA ETRC is heavy metal motor sport at its very best, a truly unique spectacle and the pinnacle of global truck competition with 2026 marking the 20th full season since the current format was introduced.  With the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) assuming full control of the series, the Goodyear FIA ETRC enters an exciting new era in 2026.  As well as continuing to oversee the Goodyear FIA ETRC’s sporting and technical regulations, the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide is taking a more hands-on approach in running the championship.  Areas such as partnerships, calendar development, circuit relations, competitor engagement and paddock operations are all being managed directly by the FIA, part of efforts to strengthen the championship’s long-term growth by covering areas from sporting level to media exposure and sustainability.   SUSTAINABILITY AT THE HEART OF GOODYEAR FIA ETRC  Back in 2021, the Goodyear FIA ETRC became the first FIA-sanctioned motor sport series to switch to fully sustainable biofuel through a partnership with TotalEnergies, which continues in 2026.  All FIA ETRC drivers use Goodyear tyres incorporating 60 per cent sustainable materials, a five per cent increase compared to 2025, achieved through the use of carefully selected ingredients, such as silica produced from waste rice husk ash and carbon black sourced from alternative feedstocks. Goodyear retreads its racing tyres into standard truck tyres, thereby avoiding the practice of disposing of racing tyres.  Italian manufacturer IVECO, which introduced its electric S-eWay as the official Goodyear FIA ETRC pace truck in 2025, also remains a key partner.   CHAMPION KISS AT THE TRIPLE AS RODRIGUES AND SMITH SHINE IN GOODYEAR FIA ETRC   Norbert Kiss celebrated winning the Goodyear FIA European Truck Racing Championship title* for a record-extending eighth time at Le Mans last Saturday before adding two further wins of a dominant season to his tally of 18 by finishing first in both Race 3 and Race 4 in the Sunday sunshine. Despite wrapping up the coveted crown in Race 1, Kiss continued his pursuit of Goodyear FIA ETRC glory during the final day of the 24 Heures Camions weekend at the famous French venue. He set a stunning lap of 2m03.820s around the 4.185-kilometre Circuit Bugatti in second qualifying to bank pole position number 12 of 2026. His qualifying best in 2025 was a 2m04.322s. The MAN-powered Révész Racing driver then secured the Race 3 win by a commanding margin of 8.801s ahead of six-time champion Jochen Hahn with Sascha Lenz finishing third to continue his push for the runner-up spot in the final title standings behind Kiss. But the Hungarian hero left his best to last when he charged through from eighth on the Race 4 reverse grid to win ahead of Chrome star Bradley Smith – who led overall for four laps – and Antonio Albacete. Points scored by Kiss and René Reinert at Le Mans ensured their Révész-Reinert Racing Team won the Goodyear FIA European Truck Racing Championship for Teams* with one round remaining. Having snatched the Goodyear FIA ETRC Chrome points lead from defending champion Mark Taylor by winning the category in Race 2, John Newell edged ahead of his British rival with a second consecutive victory in Race 3 before Smith took the honours in Race 4 having also triumphed in Race 1. Newell finished second with Taylor in third. Heading into the Jarama season showdown, Newell leads Taylor by 13 points. After winning Race 2, José Eduardo Rodrigues’ Le Mans weekend got even better when he wrapped up the Goodyear FIA ETRC Young Driver crown* in Race 3. However, the third-generation competitor from Portugal suffered a frustrating Race 4 when he ran wide and dropped back while running in second place. He recovered to 10th from 14th.   FANS GET THEIR SAY WITH NEW-FOR-2026 GOODYEAR WINGFOOT AWARD   Already presented in several major series, including the FIA World Endurance Championship, European Le Mans Series and the British Touring Car Championship, the Goodyear Wingfoot Award is new to the Goodyear FIA European Truck Racing Championship for 2026 and recognises driver performance and achievement in the Goodyear FIA ETRC. At each of the seven Goodyear FIA ETRC events, a panel of experts from the FIA and Goodyear nominate three drivers following Race 3, based on their overall performance during the race weekend, their sporting behaviour and highlights on track. Fans will then be able to vote for their driver of the weekend via   Instagram   from the shortlist of candidates during Race 4. The winner is announced as part of the live broadcast coverage of Race 4 and presented with the Goodyear Wingfoot Award on the final podium. Norbert Kiss (Misano), Sascha Lenz (Slovakia Ring), Jochen Hahn (Nürburgring), Lukas Hahn (Most), John Newell (Zolder) and Steffi Halm (Le Mans) are the winners so far. GOODYEAR FIA ETRC DRIVERS LOOK AHEAD TO JARAMA Antonio Albacete (Spain):  “For me to race at Jarama is fantastic. It’s my home race, 25 kilometres from where I live. It’s always very good to race there, it’s an old-shape circuit and quite demanding. But I like to be there and I always like to race there. It’s a little bit narrow but it’s good for truck racing. It’s a challenge with some tricky corners and also some fast ones when you come down the hill. It’s demanding and you have the heavy braking before the left-hander. It’s fantastic to win at Jarama, it’s always great, even for the fans. As we are not playing for the championship, sometimes it’s worth to finish eighth for the reverse grid. Jochen [Hahn] and me are winning there the most so there will be a fight for that title.”   Luke Garrett (Great Britain):  “Jarama has always been my favourite track, even when my dad (Ross) was racing. I love Jarama but we just haven’t had any luck there. We’ve never nailed the set-up, but I love the track when it goes up and down, the aggressive surface, the corners and the banking. I always look forward to it, but I just need a little bit of luck. Fingers crossed we’ll get that this year.”   Steffi Halm (Germany):  “I love Jarama. It’s like an old-school track, going up and down. You have some corners you don’t see the exit, so it’s a very tough track but I love driving at Jarama. Sometimes it’s worked very well, but sometimes not. It depends how you get the set-up done for the track. We’ve had some great results in the past, but for sure the most important thing is to have a good qualifying, that’s the reason why we struggled a bit this season, the qualifying was not good enough, so I hope we can finish on the podium in Jarama but not only in the reverse-grid races.”   Luis Recuenco (Spain):  “For me, Jarama is the benchmark circuit. It is the track where I have gained the most experience, it’s where I started racing in 1988, and where I have been able to put everything I have learned into practice. I am Spanish, and the circuit is very close to home. I enjoy every corner, every braking zone and every racing line. I also really enjoy the atmosphere and the people. At the end of the day, we are all from the same city, so there is a very special connection with the spectators. My goal is simply to do the best job possible. I believe that will allow me to achieve better results and, above all, to feel more fulfilled and more in tune with myself as a driver.”   José Eduardo Rodrigues (Portugal):  “Jarama is five hours from my home so it’s my home race and I feel very good in Jarama. Normally I have good results there. This year is no different and I try to push to the maximum. For me the track is not easy but I like Jarama. I’ve raced there many times, so I have a good reference there. Maybe after Zolder it’s my second favourite race track. We have a lot of fans there, Portuguese people, Spanish people so it’s very good for me and I try to be calm and try to do a good result for the fans.”   GOODYEAR FIA ETRC IN SHORT 4x7:  Seven rounds with four races per event (two races each day)  160 kph:  Safety-first approach means a speed limit of 160kph  1200bhp:  Power output of 1200bhp and torque of around 6000Nm  5300:  Minimum required racing truck total weight is 5300 kilograms, with a minimum of 3150 kilograms measured on the front axle  Qualifying format:  For Races 1 and 3 a three-stage qualifying format decides the grid: Q1/Q4: 15 minutes for all drivers; Q2/Q5: 10 minutes for the 12 fastest drivers from Q1/Q4; Q3/Q6: 5 minutes for fastest six drivers from Q2/Q5; grid positions for Races 2 and 4 decided by the results of Races 1 and 3 with the top-eight drivers lining up in reverse order  Titan or Chrome:  Drivers are either categorised as Titan or Chrome depending on their experience and level of success  Titles:  Four FIA titles for Overall and Chrome drivers, Young Driver and Teams  Goodyear Wingfoot Award:  Three drivers are nominated for the public vote on via   Instagram   during Race 4 based on their overall performance, sporting behaviour and highlights on track     GOODYEAR FIA ETRC ROUND SIX ESSENTIALS Venue:  Circuito de Madrid Jarama – RACE, Autovía A-1, km. 28, 28700 San Sebastián de los Reyes, Madrid, Spain  Website:   https://carreradecamionesjarama.es/en/   Date:  3-4 October 2026  Track length:  3.850 kilometres  Turns:  14 (8 right, 6 left)  Direction:  Clockwise  2025 winners:  Norbert Kiss x 2, Antonio Albacete x 1, John Newell x 1  Tickets:  Click   HERE   for more information  In 100 words:  Designed by John Hugenholtz, whose work included Suzuka and Zolder, Circuito de Madrid Jarama is located in San Sebastián de los Reyes, just north of the capital and was Spain’s first permanent circuit when it opened in 1967. title: F1 – Leclerc leads Hadjar and Norris in rain-threatened second practice at Sepang
summary: Sport news Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets in Free Practice 2 for the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the Ferrari driver finishing ahead of Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and McLaren’s Lando Norris at the Sepang International Circuit.  Following a dry and sunny opening practice session, the threat of rain loomed over the second hour of running, with forecasts indicating a 90 per cent chance of precipitation. As a result, all 22 drivers headed out shortly after the pit lane opened at 1600 local time, keen to gather valuable data before conditions potentially changed.  Most initially opted for the Medium tyres, although both McLaren and Cadillac drivers, alongside Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, began on the Soft compound.  Max Verstappen continued where he had left off in FP1, setting an early benchmark of 1:37.785s to lead Mercedes’ George Russell by 0.235s. Leclerc initially placed third, ahead of Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.  With rain still threatening, several drivers switched to soft tyres around 15 minutes into the session, earlier than would normally be expected. Russell and Antonelli both attempted flying laps, but neither Mercedes driver improved, with Antonelli having his time deleted for exceeding track limits.  There was also a close encounter between Hamilton and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, who took avoiding action after encountering the Ferrari moving slowly on the racing line. The incident was noted by the stewards, with Hamilton subsequently reporting visibility issues with his right-hand mirror.  As the skies began to clear, Leclerc moved to the top with a 1:37.528s, putting him 0.137s ahead of Norris, who had made set-up adjustments following a difficult opening session. Hadjar then split the pair with a 1:37.627s, leaving the top three separated by just 0.137s.  Verstappen remained on the Medium compound, while most of the field concentrated on longer runs as the session progressed. Bortoleto and Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad provided some on-track action, engaging in a prolonged battle that included several exchanges of position.  The Audi driver later asked his team to inspect the floor of his car after running wide, before bringing out the Virtual Safety Car in the closing stages when his machine stopped in the middle sector. Yellow flags were deployed with two minutes remaining, ending any prospect of late improvements.  Leclerc’s earlier effort therefore remained unbeaten, with Hadjar second and Norris third. Verstappen finished fourth, ahead of Hamilton and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who recovered from 11th in FP1 to take sixth.  Russell and Antonelli were seventh and eighth respectively, followed by Liam Lawson and Gasly completing the top 10.  Lindblad finished 11th, ahead of Bortoleto, Nico Hülkenberg, Esteban Ocon, Fernando Alonso, Oliver Bearman, Carlos Sainz, Lance Stroll, Valtteri Bottas, Alex Albon, Sergio Pérez and Franco Colapinto.   2026 FIA Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – Free Practice 2   1 Charles Leclerc Ferrari 1:37.528 29 204.605 2 Isack Hadjar Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 1:37.627 0.099 23 204.398 3 Lando Norris McLaren/Mercedes 1:37.665 0.137 25 204.318 4 Max Verstappen Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 1:37.785 0.257 20 204.068 5 Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 1:37.833 0.305 28 203.967 6 Oscar Piastri McLaren/Mercedes 1:37.899 0.371 26 203.830 7 George Russell Mercedes 1:38.020 0.492 28 203.578 8 Kimi Antonelli Mercedes 1:38.060 0.532 28 203.495 9 Liam Lawson Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1:38.496 0.968 30 202.595 10 Pierre Gasly Alpine/Mercedes 1:38.588 1.060 29 202.405 11 Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1:38.880 1.352 33 201.808 12 Gabirel Bortoleto Audi 1:39.051 1.523 25 201.459 13 Nico Hülkenberg Audi 1:39.109 1.581 30 201.341 14 Esteban Ocon Haas/Ferrari 1:39.361 1.833 29 200.831 15 Fernando Alonso Aston Martin/Honda 1:39.478 1.950 28 200.595 16 Oliver Bearman Haas/Ferrari 1:39.706 2.178 30 200.136 17 Carlos Sainz Williams/Mercedes 1:39.930 2.402 31 199.687 18 Lance Stroll Aston Martin/Honda 1:40.150 2.622 26 199.249 19 Valtteri Bottas Cadillac/Ferrari 1:40.186 2.658 27 199.177 20 Alexander Albon Williams/Mercedes 1:40.221 2.693 30 199.107 21 Sergio Pérez Cadillac/Ferrari 1:40.938 3.410 28 197.693 22 Franco Colapinto Alpine/Mercedes 1:43.391 5.863 31 193.003    FIA Formula One World Championship    F1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026F101 Friday, October 2, 2026 - 12:03pm  Friday, October 2, 2026 - 12:03pm

title: F1 - 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia - Friday Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  TEAM REPRESENTATIVES  -  James VOWLES (Williams), Frédéric VASSEUR (Ferrari), Flavio BRIATORE (Alpine)     Q: If I could start with all three of you, if that’s okay. It’s been a challenging season, with world events affecting everybody, but I’d just like to get a word from you, if I can, on the Bahrain organisers, who’ve brought the Bahrain Grand Prix experience here to Malaysia this weekend, and the huge effort that they’ve put in to make this feel as though we are at the Bahrain Grand Prix. James, if I can start with you.   James VOWLES:  Yeah, I think incredible job by them. When you walk outside, you can see actually huge amounts of the facilities from Bahrain itself that have been brought here, and it’s impressive to do that at the scale and level that they have done. For us, we obviously want to be racing as much as possible, and it’s fantastic that they’re managing this event back onto the calendar in the way it is. So well done to all of them, and hopefully normal service resuming shortly.  Frédéric VASSEUR:  Yes, not much to add. I think it’s showing the commitment of Bahrain vis-à-vis F1. It’s something unusual to do the Bahrain Grand Prix somewhere else, but it shows the effort of all the Bahrainis vis-à-vis F1. We knew for a long time that it’s like this, that we are always more than welcome when we are going to Manama, but honestly it’s exceptional.  FB:  Same. Really, thank you to the Crown Prince Salman and all the organisation, Stefano. We want to do as many races as possible. This was a fantastic idea. It’s a little bit strange, you know, to be in Malaysia, but when you arrive at the airport yesterday, it was “Welcome to Bahrain”. So basically, I think it’s a super idea. For us, it’s great to race in Malaysia.    Q: Thank you very much. Fred, if I can come to you. Ferrari felt it necessary to issue a public statement this week expressing full confidence in you. Can I ask why was that statement needed?   FV:  I think this you have to ask your colleagues. When you see the noise and all the rumours in the press all the week, I think as a team we need to work in serenity, and it was absolutely not the case. I think the statement was mandatory to do something, or it would have been the same this weekend. But honestly, the big issue that we have today is the stability, the serenity into the team, the focus that we need to have, and not to have this kind of question all the day.  JV:  I’m just going to add to that. Normally we beat each other up and put knives in our backs, but Ferrari is in the best place it’s been in the championship for a while. They have innovation on the car this year with a rear wing and exhaust blowing that we’ve all copied as a result of it. It’s a team that’s doing brilliantly. So, I mean, for me personally, there is no question that Fred is the right person to do this.  FV:  Thanks.   FB:  You’re the right lawyer.    Q: Fred, if I could continue with you. In Baku, you had to add downforce to the car because of grip issues. You weren’t able to see the full potential of that second ADUO, the power unit there. What’s your understanding of the potential of this car, and particularly at this circuit this weekend with this layout?   FV:  We knew before going to Baku that it wouldn’t be the easiest weekends of the season, that with the straight line that we have, for sure the deficit was huge. We tried to do our best so that wven if it was not an easy one, we were still on the first row. It’s not also a bad result in itself, the quali at least. And this weekend, I think it’s much more difficult to have a good understanding of what could be the weekend, that will be mega dominated by degradation. We saw this morning that it’s a completely different story compared to the last four or five weeks, when you had Monza, Madrid, Baku. We had almost zero deg. This weekend will be another story. It means that we have to change a little bit the focus and to be much more focused on the race pace.    Q: Thank you. Flavio, if I can come to you. The crash in Baku obviously cost the team dearly in that fight for fifth in the Constructors’. Can I ask, have you spoken to the drivers coming into this weekend? Have you discussed any consequences for similar incidents?   FB:  Whatever we do is internal to the team. Sure, I was very disappointed with what happened in Baku, but it’s another race. We need to forget. We need to look always for the future, and the past is the past. There’s nothing possible to do. I was upset, yes, like I believe everybody in the team, including Franco, for the mistake he made. But this is the past. We need to go ahead and think about the future. Let’s talk about the race, the qualifying tomorrow and the race Sunday. Every race is a different scenario. Last weekend was not nice for us at all, and we’re fighting for fifth position with Racing Bulls. We gave away a lot of points. After that, it’s finished. What can we do? Whatever we’ve done, it is impossible to come back.    Q: The gap now, 15 points to Racing Bulls. When both teams are essentially fighting for eighth, ninth and tenth in the championship,    FB:  I think we have seven races… or eight. James, how many .  No. Jesus Christ!
